A Single Motion Objective for BOLD, ASL, Diffusion and Slow-Flow MRI Time Series with a Re-Descending Trajectory Prior

Author: Brian B. Avants (University of Virginia)  |  Software: syntx 6.30.5, antsxdwi 0.33.x, antsxfunctional 0.23.x, antsxslowflow 2.12.x  |  Generated: 2026-10-29

Synopsis

When an MRI time series is registered to a single template volume, any frame-to-frame change in image contrast or magnetic field is misread as head motion. This includes tag-control alternation in arterial spin labeling (ASL), shell and direction changes in diffusion MRI (DWI), eddy currents, and breathing-induced magnetic field (ΔB0(t)) shifts along the phase-encode axis. We present one joint solver across BOLD, ASL, DWI, and slow-flow MRI that separates three terms: (1) true 3D rigid head pose (0000.mat), (2) phase-encode eddy and ΔB0(t) field distortions (0000_eddy.mat), and (3) contrast-locked pose bias (Dkβ). The first two are applied together to sharpen the 4D image; only the first is reported as head motion; the third is discarded. A curvature-scaled Cauchy prior (λ = 0.03) damps sub-voxel noise without shrinking real motion.

Introduction

Estimating head motion in 4D MRI requires distinguishing actual movement of the skull from two impostors that alter the image on every frame [1,2].

  • The first impostor is phase-encode field distortion. Echo-planar imaging (EPI) has low bandwidth along the phase-encode axis. As a result, residual magnetic fields from diffusion gradients (eddy currents) [3] and breathing-induced changes in lung volume (ΔB0(t) susceptibility drift) shift and shear the image pixels along the phase-encode axis even when the patient’s head is motionless.
  • The second impostor is acquisition-locked contrast change. In ASL, blood water is alternately inverted (tag) and uninverted (control). In multi-shell DWI, changing the b-value or gradient direction changes the brightness of white matter relative to cerebrospinal fluid. A registration metric comparing frames of different contrast shifts its alignment centre slightly at tissue boundaries, creating false frame-to-frame pose steps locked to the acquisition schedule.

Post-hoc filtering of a single rigid motion trace cannot solve both problems at once. If phase-encode shifts are smoothed or subtracted from a single rigid transform before resampling, the uncompensated ΔB0(t) pixel shifts blur the aligned 4D series (increasing multi-shell DWI temporal variance by +5.2 % in our ablation). Conversely, if those phase-encode shifts are left inside the rigid transform to keep the image sharp, they inflate Framewise Displacement (FD) three- to four-fold and cause stationary subjects to fail quality control. Furthermore, applying a standard convex smoothing penalty to the trajectory damps slow head drift and shrinks real head jumps (audit showed an unguided alternation filter reduced true FD on a moving phantom from 0.94 to 0.15 mm).

We resolve this dilemma by modeling the acquisition design inside one joint registration objective and splitting the output into two distinct transforms per frame (Table 1).

Methods

1. Forward Generative Model and the [0000.mat, 0000_eddy.mat] Split (Figure 1A)

Rather than registering all frames to a single arbitrary volume, the solver groups frames by their acquisition contrast level ℓ(k) (for example, each b-shell in DWI, tag versus control in ASL, or each velocity state in slow-flow MRI) and aligns frame k against its own level reference Īℓ(k)(x). For a reference-space point x (in mm), the observed image Ik is modeled as:

Ik(Ek(Pk x)) (1 + ãk⊤ p) γk ≈ Īℓ(k)(x),   Pk x = Rk(x − c) + c + tk,   Ek y = y + p(ak0 + δpe,k + ãk⊤(y − c))   (1)

Here c is the brain centre of mass and p is the unit vector along the phase-encode axis. The model separates four effects:

  • True 3D rigid head pose (Pk, written to 0000.mat): A 3D rotation Rk and translation tk representing actual movement of the skull.
  • Phase-encode field distortion (Ek, written to 0000_eddy.mat): A 1D affine displacement acting strictly along the phase-encode direction p. In diffusion MRI, switching diffusion gradient gk induces a bulk shift ak0 and linear shear/scaling ãk modeled as (ak0, ãk) = C gk, along with an intensity modulation factor 1 + ãk⊤ p (the Jacobian determinant that corrects signal pile-up and stretching) [3]. Across all modalities (BOLD, ASL, DWI, and slow-flow), breathing and shim fluctuations also cause a frame-to-frame bulk translation δpe,k along p. Because true rigid head motion produces comparable step variance on the phase-encode and readout axes whereas ΔB0(t) fluctuations act only along p, we estimate the excess phase-encode step energy above the distortion-immune readout noise floor via Wiener shrinkage and transfer δpe,k p out of tk into 0000_eddy.mat.
  • Contrast-locked pose offset (Dkβ, removed and never resampled): Each frame’s raw 6-DOF pose is parameterized as mk + Dkβ, where mk is the free head pose and Dkβ captures apparent pose shifts locked to the acquisition design Dk (level indicators plus the five even-order l = 2 spherical harmonic direction terms per DWI shell). Along p, Dkβ is projected onto the subspace orthogonal to gk so that odd-in-gk eddy shifts stay in Ek while even-in-gk contrast shifts stay in Dkβ. Because Dkβ reflects contrast differences rather than movement of the anatomy, it is subtracted before writing 0000.mat and is never applied to the image.
  • Global gain (γk): A single multiplicative scalar per frame that absorbs uniform scanner signal drift so it cannot mimic slow translation.

All frames are optimized simultaneously in PyTorch by maximizing Mattes mutual information against Īℓ(k), using coarse-to-fine Adam capture followed by full-resolution L-BFGS and a coupled Newton polish. During resampling, the two-transform chain [0000.mat, 0000_eddy.mat] is composed and applied in a single pass using pure-PyTorch float32 order-3 cardinal B-spline interpolation.

2. Curvature-Normalized Re-Descending Trajectory Prior (Figure 1B, C)

To suppress sub-voxel registration noise on low-SNR frames without flattening real head motion, we penalize the discrete second difference (acceleration) of the free head pose, ut = mt − ½(mt−1 + mt+1), where rotations are converted to millimetres on a 50 mm cortical radius. Because ut = 0 for any constant-velocity motion, steady linear head drift is never penalized. The penalty added to the objective is:

λ κ ∑t ρ(|ut|),   ρ(u) = (δ2/2) log(1 + u2/δ2),   ρ′(u) = u / (1 + u2/δ2),   δ = 0.05 mm, λ = 0.03   (2)

Two features make this prior work across diverse MRI sequences without manual tuning:

  • Curvature normalization (κ): The raw sharpness of the mutual-information loss varies widely across modalities (for example, low-contrast ASL versus high-SNR BOLD). At each stage, the solver measures the median second derivative κ (in mm−2) of the image metric with respect to translation. Multiplying λ by κ makes the weight λ = 0.03 dimensionless. In a motionless low-contrast ASL phantom, an unnormalized weight of 0.02 pulled the trajectory by 0.1 mm, whereas curvature normalization produced zero displacement.
  • Re-descending Cauchy influence function (ρ′(u)): Standard convex penalties such as Charbonnier (ρ(u) = δ√(u2 + δ2) − δ2) or steep-origin L1 (sparse, knee δ/10) exert a constant maximum pull ρ′(u) even when |ut| is large, which drags real head jumps toward the mean of neighbouring frames. In contrast, the Cauchy derivative ρ′(u) rises linearly for tiny wiggles below the knee δ = 0.05 mm, peaks at u = δ, and then re-descends toward zero (∼ δ2/u) for larger steps (Figure 1B). Thus sub-voxel noise wiggles are damped, while sudden head movements larger than a few tenths of a millimetre break free of the penalty and are estimated purely from the image data. Because the exact second derivative ρ″(u) becomes negative above δ, our coupled Newton solver uses the positive-definite iteratively reweighted least-squares (IRLS) majoriser (ρ′(u)/u) I6, solving the block-pentadiagonal system across active frames in pure-PyTorch float32.

3. Dual Phantom-and-Clinical Acceptance Gate

We did not choose the penalty form or weight by visual inspection. Instead, every candidate prior was required to pass two quantitative gates simultaneously:

  1. Ground-truth phantom gate (n = 3): Synthetic 4D series with known planted motion trajectories across ASL (drift plus jitter), multi-shell DWI (motion plus a 0.4 mm per unit g eddy shift), and slow-flow MRI (four encoding states). A candidate prior was rejected if it increased FD error against ground truth by more than 10 % on any phantom, and it was required to reduce FD error on DWI.
  2. Clinical readout-floor gate (n = 5): Unlike the phase-encode axis, the frequency-encode (readout) axis has high bandwidth and is physically immune to ΔB0(t) and eddy-current shifts. Once design-locked contrast offsets Dkβ are removed, frame-to-frame steps along the readout axis represent a physical floor of true head jitter plus irreducible image noise. On five clinical series, a prior was rejected if it shrank the readout step median absolute deviation (MAD) by more than 0.02 mm (20 μm), degraded post-correction temporal standard deviation by more than 1 %, or changed mean FD by more than 2 %.

4. Variance Ledger and Frame Censoring (FD vs. FDbandlimited)

For every series, the module syntx.motion_decomposition produces an auditable ledger in both the pose domain and the voxel intensity domain:

  • Pose step-variance shares: Along each anatomical acquisition axis (readout and phase-encode), frame-to-frame step variance is partitioned into the percentage held by true rigid head pose (0000.mat, mk), applied phase-encode distortion (0000_eddy.mat, Ek), and removed contrast-locked bias (Dkβ).
  • Voxel intensity variance shares: At foreground brain voxels, sequential Type I sums of squares (after factoring out γk) measure the percentage of temporal variance explained by the acquisition design (level means plus l = 2, 4 DWI directional terms), by the 6-DOF motion regressors after accounting for the design, and by the unexplained residual, both before (raw) and after motion correction.
  • Complementary role of FD and FDbandlimited: Primary Framewise Displacement FD(mk) is computed on a 50 mm radius from 0000.mat alone, so it is already free of phase-encode ΔB0(t) and eddy pseudomotion at any repetition time (TR). In fast acquisitions (TR ≤ 2.78 s, T ≥ 32, such as 1.0 s BOLD), breathing also causes a real mechanical head nod in the sagittal plane (slice translation tz and pitch rx at 0.18–0.50 Hz). Because this nod is real movement of the skull, it remains in 0000.mat for spatial resampling; however, summing its ±0.20 mm oscillation on every 1 s frame inflates step-wise scrubbing rates. When a narrowband spectral peak (prominence ≥ 1.5) is detected in 0.18–0.50 Hz, FDbandlimited applies a cosine-tapered notch filter to the pose traces before differencing [2,4] so frame censoring targets sporadic head jerks rather than steady breathing.

5. Datasets

We evaluated the solver (syntx 6.30.5) on five clinical reference series: (1) resting-state BOLD (T = 300, TR 1.0 s, phase-encode j−), (2) 25-volume ASL with M0 calibration (TR 4.0 s), (3) 60-volume PCASL without M0 (30 tag/control pairs, TR 4.4 s), (4) 100-volume multi-shell DWI (b = 1500/3000 s/mm2, dir-AP), and (5) 99-volume low-SNR multi-shell DWI (b = 1500/3000 s/mm2, dir-PA). We also evaluated a 200-volume multi-shell DWI scan with severe eddy/ΔB0(t) distortion (sub-EAS024) and an independent four-run task-fMRI dataset (OpenNeuro ds007693, sub-07, 4 × 340 = 1360 volumes, TR 1.5 s).

Results

1. Only the Re-Descending Cauchy Prior at λ = 0.03 Passes Both the Phantom and Clinical Gates (Figure 2)

We first tested the intuition that small frame-to-frame second differences should be penalized most aggressively using the steep-origin sparse penalty and the convex Charbonnier penalty. On a 1D synthetic curve with Gaussian noise (Figure 1C), sparse at unit weight removed 71 % of sub-knee jitter energy compared with 54 % for Charbonnier and 53 % for Cauchy. However, on the 3D ground-truth phantoms (Figure 2A), both non-redescending penalties failed badly: at λ = 0.10, sparse increased FD error by +86 % on ASL and +55 % on slow-flow MRI, and Charbonnier increased FD error by +70 % and +50 %, because both penalties smoothed away true sub-voxel motion planted in the phantom trajectories.

Only the re-descending Cauchy form passed the phantom gate, reducing FD error by −14 % on ASL, −17 % on DWI, and −3 % on slow-flow at λ = 0.03 (and by −7 %, −27 %, and +3 % at λ = 0.05). The clinical readout-floor gate (Figure 2B, C) then separated the two weights: at λ = 0.05, Cauchy over-smoothed the B0-immune readout trace on the 100-volume DWI series, reducing the readout step MAD by 0.043 mm (from 0.081 to 0.038 mm, exceeding the 0.020 mm gate). At λ = 0.03, every clinical series stayed inside both acceptance bands (maximum readout step change 0.011 mm; image alignment unchanged within ≤ 0.1 %; FD change within −0.9 to +1.8 %). We therefore unified λ = 0.03 as the default across all one-level and multi-level designs.

2. Separating [0000.mat, 0000_eddy.mat] Eliminates False Phase-Encode FD While Sharpening 4D Alignment (Table 2, Figure 3)

Table 2 and Figure 3 report the complete pose and voxel variance decomposition across the five clinical series:

  • Multi-shell DWI (T = 100 and T = 99, plus sub-EAS024 T = 200): On the phase-encode axis, applied eddy and ΔB0(t) shifts in 0000_eddy.mat account for 87 % and 93 % of the total frame-to-frame step variance, removed contrast-locked offsets Dkβ account for 7 % and 3 %, and true rigid head motion in 0000.mat accounts for less than 1 %. On the B0-immune readout axis, Dkβ accounts for 68 % and 87 % of the step variance (from l = 2 directional contrast shifts across shells), while true head motion accounts for 38 % and 9 %. Because earlier pipelines left the centered eddy and ΔB0(t) phase-encode translations inside 0000.mat, they reported mean FD of 0.60 mm (44 % of volumes > 0.50 mm) and 0.48 mm (36 % > 0.50 mm) on these two series. Transferring those phase-encode field shifts into 0000_eddy.mat reduces mean rigid FD to 0.14 mm (0 % > 0.50 mm) and 0.15 mm (1 % > 0.50 mm) while applying the exact same total displacement during B-spline resampling. On the 200-volume sub-EAS024 DWI scan, mean rigid FD similarly fell from 0.474 mm (71/200 volumes > 0.50 mm) to 0.173 mm (0/200 volumes > 0.50 mm) while keeping 0.680 mm RMS eddy shear and 0.303 mm RMS ΔB0(t) shift in 0000_eddy.mat. In the voxel domain, motion correction increases variance explained by the diffusion design from 94.3 to 96.2 % and from 90.8 to 95.6 %, cuts motion contamination after design from 0.57 to 0.45 % and from 1.76 to 0.66 %, and leaves the residual uncorrelated with FD (r = −0.09 and −0.04).
  • Resting-state BOLD (T = 300, TR 1.0 s): Even without diffusion gradients, breathing-induced ΔB0(t) field shifts along the phase-encode axis (j−) account for 53 % of the raw phase-encode step variance. Moving δpe,k into 0000_eddy.mat reduces the phase-encode step SD in 0000.mat by 92.3 % in variance (from 0.140 mm down to 0.039 mm, matching the 0.047 mm readout noise floor) and lowers mean Power FD from 0.60 to 0.55 mm (38 % > 0.50 mm). The remaining step variance in 0000.mat is dominated by real mechanical respiratory head nodding in the sagittal plane (slice tz step SD 0.377 mm and pitch rx step SD 0.193 mm oscillating at 0.48 Hz, prominence 1.94, holding 56.3 % of band power). Self-gated FDbandlimited notches this 0.355–0.50 Hz breathing band for censoring, reducing mean censoring FD to 0.28 mm and censored frames from 38 % to 11 %, while voxel motion variance falls from 36.41 to 25.62 %.
  • Arterial Spin Labeling (T = 25 with M0 and T = 60 PCASL): Separating phase-encode ΔB0(t) shifts into 0000_eddy.mat accounts for 52 % and 56 % of phase-encode step variance, lowering mean rigid FD from 0.51 to 0.47 mm on the 25-volume series and from 0.19 to 0.16 mm (2 % censored) on the 60-volume series. On the 25-volume series, tag/control+M0 design variance rises from 97.0 to 98.3 % and motion variance after design drops by half (0.35 to 0.18 %).
  • Execution speed: Vectorizing the coupled Newton active-frame Cholesky solver and order-3 B-spline resampling in pure-PyTorch float32 (and reusing the single-pass reference mask) reduced total wall-clock time across the five clinical series from 777 s (66 to 229 s per series) to 227 s (31 to 69 s per series, 3.4× faster).

Discussion

Our results demonstrate why phase-encode distortion correction and head-motion reporting must be decoupled into two separate transform files ([0000.mat, 0000_eddy.mat]) rather than forced into one. On multi-shell DWI, 87 to 93 % of phase-encode step variance and 68 to 87 % of readout step variance are driven by eddy currents, ΔB0(t) field drift, and shell/direction contrast rather than movement of the skull. If an algorithm forces the applied phase-encode translation to be temporally smooth, real frame-to-frame ΔB0(t) voxel shifts go uncorrected during resampling and blur the shells; if an algorithm keeps those shifts inside a single rigid transform, the resampled image is sharp but the reported FD trace reflects field distortion rather than patient motion. Writing the rigid skull pose to 0000.mat and the phase-encode eddy plus ΔB0(t) shifts to 0000_eddy.mat solves both problems across all time-series modalities.

Equally important, our phantom and clinical gates falsified two plausible regularization hypotheses. First, penalties with steep origin pull (sparse) or constant large-step pull (Charbonnier) removed the most noise on a 1D toy curve but degraded 3D phantom accuracy by 50 to 86 % because they smoothed real motion steps. Second, amplitude shrinkage toward the identity transform (pose_shrinkage) lowered clinical FD by 11 to 41 % within the readout floor but increased ASL drift-phantom error two- to three-fold by pulling drifting heads toward zero. Only a curvature-normalized, re-descending second-difference prior (λ = 0.03) preserved both linear drift and real jumps while damping sub-voxel noise.

Limitations. (1) Our 3D phantom generators plant sub-knee jitter in the ground-truth motion trajectory rather than synthesizing independent thermal noise across image repetitions; a dedicated k-space/image-noise phantom gate is needed next. (2) On the 60-volume PCASL series without an M0 volume, the tag-control design explains only 1.1 % of voxel variance while motion regressors explain 53.75 %, reflecting strong spatial coupling between perfusion contrast and slice-wise signal changes that pose regression alone does not separate. (3) Censoring thresholds (0.50 mm in antsxqc) have not yet been benchmarked against downstream test-retest connectivity or tractography reproducibility on these five series. (4) An alternative engine that projects design columns inside the image metric (engine="projected") over-reports B0-immune readout jitter on real multi-shell DWI (0.145 vs. 0.080 mm) and is therefore not used by default. (5) Any true physical head motion that oscillates at the exact frequency of the acquisition design (for example, Nyquist tag-control alternation) lies in the column space of Dk and is indistinguishable from Dkβ.

Novelty Assessment

What builds on prior work. Using mutual information to reduce sensitivity to activation contrast follows Freire and Mangin [1]. Modeling diffusion eddy currents along the phase-encode axis as a gradient-linear affine with Jacobian intensity modulation follows Andersson and Sotiropoulos [3]. Filtering respiratory oscillations from framewise displacement before scrubbing follows Power et al. [2] and Fair et al. [4].

What is new in this contribution.

  1. Universal [0000.mat, 0000_eddy.mat] split and Dkβ contrast removal across BOLD, ASL, DWI, and slow-flow MRI: A single joint solver separates true 3D rigid head pose (0000.mat), applied phase-encode eddy and Wiener-shrunk ΔB0(t) field shifts (0000_eddy.mat, resampled together in one pure-PyTorch float32 B-spline pass), and unapplied contrast-locked pose bias (Dkβ).
  2. Curvature-normalized re-descending Cauchy prior (λ = 0.03) with active-frame IRLS Newton optimization: Normalizing the second-difference penalty by stage-wise median translation curvature κ makes λ = 0.03 invariant to image contrast, while the re-descending Cauchy pull damps sub-knee (< 0.05 mm) wiggles without shrinking drift or jumps.
  3. Dual ground-truth phantom and B0-immune readout-floor acceptance gate: Combining synthetic drifting phantoms with the physical requirement that regularization must not shrink steps along the distortion-immune readout axis (< 20 μm) falsified convex L1/Charbonnier priors, amplitude shrinkage, and over-weighted Cauchy (λ = 0.05).
  4. Closed-form pose and voxel variance ledger (syntx.motion_decomposition): Quantifies the exact percentage of step variance and voxel intensity variance attributable to rigid head motion, applied phase-encode distortion, and removed contrast bias in every scan.

Conclusion

Across BOLD, ASL, multi-shell diffusion, and slow-flow MRI, a single joint objective with a λ = 0.03 re-descending Cauchy prior separates applied transforms into [0000.mat, 0000_eddy.mat] and removes contrast-locked bias Dkβ—producing sharp 4D volumes and uncontaminated head-motion FD traces 3.4× faster.
